## Results

Two scenarios from the zap/zerolog convention (static string / 10 fields),
benched against the Go stdlib baseline `log/slog` on the same scenarios. Both
loggers write to a `discardSink` so the I/O is out of the measurement.

```
BenchmarkLoggerStaticString-8   	 558814	  410.0 ns/op	  64 B/op	1 allocs/op
BenchmarkSlogStaticString-8     	 628737	  386.6 ns/op	   0 B/op	0 allocs/op
BenchmarkLogger10Fields-8       	 301843	  833.2 ns/op	 768 B/op	1 allocs/op
BenchmarkSlog10Fields-8         	 208262	 1055.0 ns/op	 208 B/op	1 allocs/op
```

## How to read this

- **Latency (ns/op).** Our logger beats slog on the 10-fields scenario (833 vs 1055 ns/op, ~26% faster). On static strings slog is marginally ahead (387 vs 410 ns/op).
- **Allocations.** The variadic `logger.Info(ctx, lg, "msg", attrs...)` path costs **1 alloc/op** (the variadic slice). Slog's static-string path costs 0 allocs because the call site has no variadic. The CLAUDE.md "zero-alloc" claim describes the chainable **`Build(lg, lv).Str(...).Send(...)`** path, which goes through a `sync.Pool`-backed builder — not this convenience variadic. If your hot path matters more than ergonomics, prefer Build.
- **Bytes per op.** On 10 fields we allocate more (768 vs 208) — this is the 10-attr slice (10 `AttrValue`s × ~76 B each). Slog packs more tightly in its variadic encoder.

## Caveats

- `zap` / `zerolog` are NOT included here — that's a deliberate scope decision (adding them would require pulling them into `pkg/v1/logger`'s `go.mod`). The slog comparison is the most honest stdlib baseline.
- Single run, no `benchstat -count=5` variance indicator. Treat numbers as ±10%.
- The discard sink is synchronous; multi-sink / async middleware would shift the picture (those are tested separately).

## Methodology

- `cd pkg/v1 && go test -run '^$' -bench=. -benchmem -benchtime=200ms ./logger`
- Both loggers initialised once outside the bench loop; the loop is `b.N` calls to `.Info(...)`.
